candidate.answerReason: Triangles ABE and DCE have the same angle at E. Their remaining angle sums are therefore equal, giving \(S=S'>0\) and \(r=1\).

methods.label: Method 1: Compare two triangles
methods.explanation:
The extensions place \(A,D,E\) in that order on one line and \(B,C,E\) in that order on another. Thus triangles \(ABE\) and \(DCE\) share the same angle at \(E\).

Let \(\theta\) be the degree measure of this common angle. In triangle \(ABE\), the angles at \(A\) and \(B\) are precisely \(\angle BAD\) and \(\angle ABC\), so
\[
S'=180-\theta.
\]
In triangle \(DCE\), the other two angles have sum
\[
S=180-\theta.
\]
Consequently \(S=S'\). These are nondegenerate triangles, so \(S'>0\), and
\[
r=\frac{S}{S'}=1.
\]
The answer is choice E.
methods.levelReason: Only the stated point order and the elementary triangle angle sum are used.

methods.label: Method 2: Use supplementary angles
methods.explanation:
Let \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\) be the interior angle measures, in degrees, of the convex quadrilateral at \(A,B,C,D\), respectively. Its interior angle sum gives
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=360.
\]
Because \(DE\) extends \(AD\) through \(D\), the angle \(CDE\) measures \(180-\delta\). Similarly, \(DCE\) measures \(180-\gamma\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=(180-\delta)+(180-\gamma)\\
&=360-\gamma-\delta\\
&=\alpha+\beta=S'.
\end{aligned}
\]
Convexity ensures \(\alpha,\beta>0\), so the denominator \(S'\) is positive. Hence \(r=S/S'=1\), choice E.
methods.levelReason: This uses the quadrilateral interior angle sum and adjacent supplementary angles.
